q7.answer: The shared state is in Redis: a sorted set presence:doc with one member per connection (score = last heartbeat time), and a hash cursors:doc with one field per connId holding that connection's last caret. The user list is not stored; it is the distinct userIds among live members. Each member is refreshed by its owning node every 10 s (ZADD plus EXPIRE 60 on both keys), and stale members are removed by a sweep every 5 s once their score is older than 30 s.

q8.answer: The surviving nodes' 5 s sweeps remove the dead node's members (score older than 30 s) and delete their cursor fields, then re-read the live members. Each surviving node then sends presence_users to its own local sockets, so clients on every live node are told; the crashed node itself does nothing. Gap I did not spell out: the design does not state that a sweep sends cursor_gone for the removed connIds, so clients may keep a stale caret until a fresh snapshot or presence update clears it.

q9.answer: The node that accepted the cursor writes it to the cursors:doc hash and publishes it on cursor:doc. Every node subscribed to cursor:doc (any node with a local socket on that document) forwards it to its local sockets, so a viewer on another node receives it through Redis pub/sub. The sender's own node receives its own publish through the same subscription and forwards it to its local viewers.

q10.answer: The joining node subscribes to presence:doc and cursor:doc before it writes its member or reads the snapshot, and it holds live frames until presence_snapshot has been sent. Anything that happens during loading is therefore either in the snapshot or arrives as a live frame, and overlap can only repeat messages. Repeats are harmless: presence_users is a full list, and cursor repeats are discarded by the seq rule.

q11.answer: Right after its open completes, each client sends one cursor, so an idle user's caret is stored in the cursors:doc hash, which the joiner reads with HGETALL and receives in presence_snapshot. Cursor entries are refreshed by heartbeat and only removed on clean close or sweep, so an idle user keeps their caret and it draws on join.

q12.answer: Each receiver keeps the highest seq seen per connId and discards any cursor with a seq lower than or equal to it. A held caret is replaced only by a higher seq, and since the sender's seq only increases, a late message cannot move a caret back to an earlier position.
